result:
The concept of "liminal space" has been thoroughly digested by the internet over the last few years, reduced mostly to grainy photographs of empty shopping malls at 3:00 AM, fluorescent-lit hotel hallways, and abandoned playgrounds coated in a thin layer of fog. Yet, the reason the concept caught fire in the collective consciousness is because it gave a name to a deeply human, nearly universal sensation: the eerie, buzzing quiet of the "in-between." 

When we strip away the aesthetic trends, liminality is actually the defining feature of the human experience. We like to believe our lives are a series of solid states—child, student, worker, partner, retiree; here, there; asleep, awake. In reality, we spend almost all of our time in the threshold between what has ended and what has not yet begun. 

Consider the airport at dawn. It is perhaps the ultimate modern monument to the in-between. Outside the towering glass walls, the tarmac is bruised with the indigo light of early morning. Inside, the normal rules of society are temporarily suspended. You will see a businessman in a tailored suit eating a plate of nachos and drinking a pale lager at 6:15 AM, and nobody blinks an eye. Next to him, a college student sleeps flat on their back on a remarkably hostile carpet, using a canvas backpack as a pillow. Time does not work properly here. You are no longer in the city you left—you have surrendered your keys, hugged your friends, and mentally checked out—but you have not yet arrived at your destination. For a few hours, you exist in a vacuum of pure potential and mild anxiety. You are nobody, going somewhere. 

There is a profound, paradoxical comfort in these spaces of suspension. Because you cannot actually *do* anything while waiting to board Flight 402, or while sitting in the sterile stillness of a doctor’s waiting room, or while driving through the hypnotic darkness of an interstate highway at midnight, you are temporarily absolved of the burden of productivity. In the liminal space, your only job is to wait. And in that waiting, the armor we wear to navigate our daily routines often slips off.

Have you ever noticed how the most honest conversations happen in cars at night? There is something about the dashboard glow, the rhythmic thrum of tires over asphalt joints, and the fact that neither person has to make eye contact. Both passengers are staring forward into the tunnel of the headlights. The world outside the windows is reduced to passing streaks of sodium-vapor orange and shadows. Because you are suspended between point A and point B, the consequences of confession feel softened. Secrets, fears, and wild philosophies spill out into the cabin air, held safely within the moving steel box, only to evaporate the moment the car pulls into a driveway and the engine is switched off. Once the door opens, you are back in a "place," and the gravity of reality returns.

Seasons have their own thresholds, too. There is a specific week in late October or early November—depending on where you live—when autumn has largely spent its theatrical budget of golds and crimsons, leaving the trees mostly bare, like charcoal sketches against a pewter sky. Yet, the true, biting freeze of winter hasn’t locked the ground just yet. The air smells of damp earth, woodsmoke, and decay. Walking through a park at dusk during this week feels like walking through a theater after the audience has left and the stagehands have packed up the set, leaving only the ghost light burning at center stage. Nature is holding its breath. 

We experience this internally just as acutely. Think of the time between quitting a job and starting a new one, or the weeks following the end of a long relationship before you have figured out how to arrange your furniture—and your identity—for one person instead of two. Psychologists and anthropologists often break these transitions into three phases: the separation from the old life, the liminal period of ambiguity, and the reincorporation into a new life. 

Our culture is notoriously bad at handling that middle phase. We worship the pivot, the glow-up, the grand arrival. We want the breakup on Friday and the inspiring montage of self-improvement to begin on Monday. We dread the formless, murky soup of the middle—the part where the caterpillar isn’t even a caterpillar anymore, nor is it a butterfly, but rather a literal sack of biological goo inside a chrysalis, entirely dissolved and rearranging itself at a cellular level. 

Being biological goo is deeply uncomfortable. It feels like failure. In the modern world, where we are constantly asked to define, brand, and broadcast who we are, admitting that you are currently *no one in particular* feels transgressive. Yet, nothing new can be built while the old structure is still occupying the lot. The demolition and the empty, dusty crater that follows are not interruptions to the building process; they *are* the building process.

Perhaps this is why we are also drawn to physical ruins and forgotten architecture. When you walk through an overgrown greenhouse or look at an old highway bypassed by a newer interstate, where dandelions are cracking through the faded yellow center lines, you are looking at time made visible. We spend so much energy maintaining the illusion of permanence. We paint our houses, pave our roads, update our software, and dye our grey hairs to convince ourselves that the present moment is a fortress that can hold out against change. 

Abandoned spaces gently mock that illusion. They remind us that everything is in transit. The shopping mall that was once the bustling heart of teenage social life in 1994 is now a quiet cavern where rainwater drips into an empty fountain. It is transitioning from a monument of commerce back into dirt and weeds, just as the dirt and weeds once transitioned into a parking lot. 

Even the micro-moments of our days are stitched together by tiny thresholds. The thirty seconds after your alarm goes off, when you cannot remember what day of the week it is or what problems you were worried about yesterday. The deep, resonant silence of a kitchen late at night when you’ve gone down for a glass of water, standing barefoot on the cold tile, listening to the hum of the refrigerator. The pause at the top of a Ferris wheel when the chair swings gently in the wind, the fairground reduced to miniature lights below you.

If we pay attention to these moments, rather than rushing through them with our eyes glued to our phones to distract ourselves from the stillness, they offer a rare kind of grace. They remind us that life is not a series of destinations interrupted by annoying commutes. Rather, the commute—the strange, uncertain, dimly lit corridor between who we were five minutes ago and who we are about to become—is where the actual living happens. We are all just waiting at the gate, watching the sky lighten over the tarmac, carrying whatever fits in a single bag, getting ready to fly.
